topic: doj approves paramount skydance warner bros deal
headline_marked: [[DoJ approves Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery deal]], cementing Ellison family control of American media
headline: DoJ approves Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery deal, cementing Ellison family control of American media
summary: The deal, backed by Larry Ellison's $45.7 billion equity, drastically expands the Ellison family's influence, creating a media portfolio to rival Disney's. It includes Warner Bros. Studios, HBO, CNN, and Warner Bros. Games.
details: The US Department of Justice has approved Paramount Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. This landmark deal, backed by $45.7 billion in equity from Oracle founder Larry Ellison, significantly consolidates American media. It expands the Ellison family's influence, creating a media portfolio comparable to Disney's.

The DoJ dismissed arguments against the merger, including comparisons to Disney's acquisition of Fox, citing the COVID-19 pandemic as an interfering factor. It also disregarded labor concerns widely voiced by industry workers. The UK is also conducting its own investigation, potentially accelerating the DoJ's timeline.

With this acquisition, Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison will oversee Warner Bros. Studios, HBO, HBO Max, CNN Worldwide, and Warner Bros. Games. This adds to their existing holdings, which include Paramount, CBS, MTV, BET, and Nickelodeon.

The deal has sparked fear over the future of the film, television, and news industries. Concerns are particularly high for CNN, given recent controversies at CBS News under Ellison control, where Bari Weiss was installed as head and made significant changes.

At CBS News, Weiss notably fired 60 Minutes correspondent Scott Pelley, leading to claims that the show was being "murdered." A 60 Minutes report on ICE facilities was scuttled, and correspondent Cecelia Vega was fired while working on a sensitive report, with her journalistic work withheld.

CBS also moved to cancel The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, a decision Paramount Skydance attributed to financial realities. This followed a Colbert segment critical of a $16 million settlement paid to former president Donald Trump by CBS.

Over 5,500 movie and television industry professionals, including notable Hollywood figures like Glenn Close and Jane Fonda, signed an open letter. They warned that the acquisition would "threaten the sustainability of the entire creative community."

While the DoJ approval was a major hurdle, state attorneys general in California and New York intend to challenge the deal. Investigations by European officials and the UK are also ongoing. Paramount Skydance faces a September 30 deadline to close the deal, after which a $7 million daily ticking fee will apply to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders.

topic: ffmpeg twenty one zero day vulnerabilities
headline_marked: [[21 zero-days discovered in FFmpeg]] by autonomous security agent, some latent for 20 years
headline: 21 zero-days discovered in FFmpeg by autonomous security agent, some latent for 20 years
summary: Depthfirst's autonomous security agent found 21 zero-day vulnerabilities in FFmpeg, a widely deployed media library. Some of these critical flaws had been latent for up to 20 years, with 8 already assigned CVEs.
details: Depthfirst's autonomous security agent has uncovered 21 zero-day vulnerabilities in FFmpeg, a critical media processing library. This discovery was made at a fraction of the cost of previous manual or AI-assisted efforts, with some flaws dating back 15 to 20 years. The agent produced concrete, reproducible Proof-of-Concept (PoC) inputs to confirm its findings for about $1,000.

FFmpeg is one of the most widely deployed software components globally, powering everything from web browsers to major streaming platforms. As a library that routinely parses complex and untrusted media, it is inherently security-critical and a prime target for zero-click attacks. Its pervasive use makes these vulnerabilities particularly impactful.

The FFmpeg codebase is massive, comprising approximately 1.5 million lines of heavily optimized C code, and has undergone two decades of relentless fuzzing and manual audits. Even with recent efforts by Google's Big Sleep team (13 vulnerabilities) and Anthropic's Mythos model (some issues), finding new bugs has become increasingly difficult.

Depthfirst built a specialized agentic system designed for deep scans over large codebases, aiming to surpass previous findings. While not having access to proprietary models like Mythos, their system successfully rediscovered known issues and, more importantly, identified new critical bugs that others had missed. This demonstrates the capability of their security system.

Unlike general coding agents, a security agent has a narrower, targeted goal: to find real, exploitable security issues in an existing system without specific instructions. It focuses on edge cases and adversarial inputs, rather than just writing functional code. This specialized approach allows for a deeper, more focused analysis of potential weaknesses.

The agent begins by threat modeling the codebase, identifying exposed parsers and mapping attacker-controlled input paths. It then audits the attack surface, tracing data flow through relevant components. Crucially, it includes guardrails to prevent false positives and fabrications, ensuring that suspected flaws are reproducible and exploitable.

In total, the agents discovered 21 zero-days across various FFmpeg components, from the TS demuxer to the VP9 decoder. Eight of these issues have already been assigned CVEs, confirming their severity and official recognition. The remaining vulnerabilities are also fixed, pending CVE identifiers.
